clue.text: Can impale things, perhaps, in the office

definitions.text: Can impale things, perhaps, in the office

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters of the opening three words may be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A warning about some office gadget that can skewer whatever is put in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges CAN IMPALE THINGS into the answer, and the whole clue describes what the device does to sheets of paper on a desk.
explanation.definitionFit: An office stapler drives a metal wire through papers, piercing them to bind them together.

clue.text: Bribe the society of magicians? Impossible task!

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase; the answer is the idiom for attempting such a thing

parts.note: to square someone is to buy them off
the Magic Circle is the British society of conjurors

explanation.surface: Someone plans to pay off a club of conjurors and is told it cannot be done.
explanation.walkthrough: The Magic Circle is Britain's best-known society of stage magicians. Squaring the circle, building a square equal in area to a circle with ruler and compass, was proved impossible.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from a geometric construction proved unachievable, so it names any hopeless undertaking.

clue.text: Stout staff required for a pub sign

parts.note: stout is a dark beer, a kind of ale
a staff is a long stick or pole

explanation.surface: A sturdy stick is needed to hang the inn's signboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stout' looks like an adjective for the staff, but it is a noun: the dark beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Alehouses once advertised by setting up a tall post bearing a bush or signboard outside.

clue.text: Legal right to hold property -said to be acceptable to 24?

indicators.note: said tells us the word we want is only heard, and is written differently

parts.note: 24 is Jack Sprat, who could eat no fat, so only lean meat suited him

explanation.surface: A lawyer's note on a property claim with an odd cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme says Jack Sprat could eat no fat, so meat acceptable to him is lean, which sounds like the legal term.
explanation.definitionFit: A lien lets a creditor keep possession of goods until a debt owed on them is paid.

clue.text: Old remedy for guitarist with sore fingers?

definitions.meaning: a quack cure or patent medicine of former times
a player with tender fingertips must give up strumming, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into NO STRUM, the instruction for a player whose fingers hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum was a secret or quack medicine; for the sore guitarist, no strumming is the prescription.

clue.text: Gains control over teachers

definitions.meaning: to get the better of or become expert in something
schoolmasters, as in a school's staff

explanation.definitionFit: To master a skill is to conquer it, while schoolmasters are the staff of a boys' school.

clue.text: Not a fair copy

parts.note: a fair copy is a clean final version; the other kind of copy is an illicit one, such as a cheat sheet or plagiarised translation

explanation.definitionFit: Schoolchildren's slang for a cheat's key or a plagiarised piece of work, copied unfairly.

clue.text: Laying it on pretty thick in the studio?

definitions.text: Laying it on pretty thick in the studio?

parts.words: Laying it on pretty thick in the studio?
parts.note: the idiom for exaggerating is read literally, as a painter applying paint in heavy layers

explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the painting technique of applying pigment so thickly that brush or knife marks stand out.

clue.text: My yellow bloomers look best as it gets dark

definitions.text: My yellow bloomers look best as it gets dark

parts.words: My yellow bloomers look best as it gets dark
parts.note: bloomers are flowers, not underwear; the plant's yellow blossoms open at dusk

explanation.definitionFit: This plant's pale yellow flowers open in the late afternoon and evening, hence its name.

clue.text: Futile advice to the prodigal?

definitions.meaning: a spendthrift should be told to consume less, read as two words

explanation.definitionFit: Something pointless is of no value; split in two, the word tells a wastrel to cut back.

clue.text: Second alcoholic drink makes one paint dotty

parts.note: a tipple is a drink of something alcoholic

explanation.surface: A second glass of booze sends an artist round the bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dotty' suggests mad, but here it means in dots.
explanation.definitionFit: Stippling is applying paint or ink in small dots rather than strokes.

clue.text: Highest position of showy violinist?

parts.note: the violinist of the show is the Fiddler of the musical, who is perched on top of a house

explanation.definitionFit: The top of a house; the musical Fiddler on the Roof puts its violinist up there.

clue.text: Contracted pair even carry themselves carefully

parts.note: PR is the short form of pair
e'en is the poetic contraction of even, the contracting carried over

explanation.surface: A couple, though abbreviated, still hold themselves with great poise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contracted' shortens both words: pair to PR, even to the poetic E'EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Birds and vain people groom and pride themselves, taking great care over their appearance.

clue.text: Sparkling wine used in Calphurnia's time

indicators.note: used in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A fizzy drink served in the days of Caesar's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Asti spumante is a sweet sparkling white from Piedmont in Italy.

clue.text: Twilled cotton — that's the stuff to give the troops

definitions.text: that's the stuff to give the troops

explanation.definitionFit: Drill is a hard-wearing twill cloth, and also the marching exercise soldiers are put through.

clue.text: As lucky as Bunter in the tuckshop?

definitions.meaning: Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of the Greyfriars stories, would be smeared with preserves at the school sweetshop

explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the gluttonous fat boy of British school stories; a tuckshop is a school snack shop.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for fortunate, and also literally covered in fruit preserve.

clue.text: Difficult to prove, the more complex it is

definitions.text: Difficult to prove, the more complex it is

indicators.note: complex says the letters of the two words are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: A mathematician grumbles that harder propositions are tougher to establish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' rearranges THE MORE, and the whole clue describes a hard mathematical proposition.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorem is a statement in mathematics that must be established by proof.

clue.text: Shanty to add flavour at Gateshead?

parts.note: to season food is to flavour it
read as Gate's head, the first letter of gate

explanation.surface: A sailors' song about spicing up food in a north-east England town.
explanation.walkthrough: Gateshead is a town on the Tyne; split as Gate's head, it gives G.
explanation.definitionFit: A shanty is a work song sung by sailors at sea.

clue.text: Oils pen, unusually, to write letter from Greece

indicators.note: unusually says the letters of the two words appear in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: An artist dips a pen in oil to write home from Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth character of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Winding down — like Gray's herd on Sunday?

parts.note: Gray's Elegy opens with the lowing herd winding slowly over the lea

explanation.surface: Cattle meandering home on a Sunday evening, as in the poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard has 'The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea'; lowing is mooing.
explanation.definitionFit: Reducing speed, easing off as something comes to an end.

clue.text: Threadbare-—that describes the insomniac

definitions.meaning: worn so the raised fibres of the cloth have gone
someone who cannot sleep gets no doze

explanation.definitionFit: Worn cloth has lost its pile, and one who cannot sleep goes without any short doze.

clue.text: Person trying some embroidery work

definitions.meaning: one who tastes or tests a portion
a piece of needlework showing a range of stitches

explanation.definitionFit: One who tastes a little of things, and a cloth panel stitched to display needlework skills.

clue.text: Person disliked need not be specified

definitions.meaning: a placeholder for something left unnamed

explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism for an unpleasant individual, and a stand-in phrase when particulars are left out.

clue.text: Played as one of three Beethoven overtures — or alone, possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests the two words could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: A concert programme note about Beethoven played by a soloist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Played' looks like the anagram signal, but it is a link; 'possibly' rearranges OR ALONE.
explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven wrote three overtures named after the heroine of his opera Fidelio, numbered one to three.

clue.text: Driver reversing in Bognor intersection

indicators.note: reversing says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A motorist backing up at a junction in a seaside town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks the letters NORI spanning BogNOR Intersection; 'reversing' turns them round. Bognor Regis is an English seaside town.
explanation.definitionFit: A driver and the answer are both golf clubs, one standing for the other as a kind of club.

clue.text: Nurseryman Jack a cholecystitis sufferer?

parts.note: the Jack of a nursery rhyme could eat no fat, as a person with gallbladder disease is told

explanation.walkthrough: Cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, whose sufferers must avoid fatty food, like the rhyme's Jack.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery rhyme's Jack could eat no fat, just as patients with gallbladder trouble cannot.

clue.text: Class distinction?

parts.note: a class in a British school is distinguished by a year name, and good manners are also good this

explanation.definitionFit: A school year group in Britain, as in sixth; also proper etiquette, as in good or bad manners.

clue.text: High-water, thanks to the fleet…

parts.note: ta is British slang for thank you
RN is the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: Gratitude to the navy for some water at altitude.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarn is a small mountain lake, water lying high up in the hills.

clue.text: …deep water, for the most part

definitions.meaning: mostly, as in the phrase in the ___

explanation.definitionFit: A poetic name for the high sea, and the word completing 'in the ___', meaning mostly.

clue.text: See ace inch round this obstacle at Brand's Hatch

indicators.note: round says the letters of the two words are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: A driver edging a top car past a hazard at a racing circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Brands Hatch is a motor-racing circuit in Kent, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A chicane is a tight series of bends put in a racing track to slow cars.

clue.text: Devil of a sticky game!

parts.note: the toy spun on a string between two sticks takes its name from the Italian for devil, and 'sticky' means played with sticks

explanation.definitionFit: A juggling toy, a double cone spun and tossed on a string tied between two hand sticks.

clue.text: Village fête event — Coe's grandpa gone round in it?

indicators.note: round says the letters of the words before it are turned about into a new order

parts.note: the letters as written, the S of Coe's included

explanation.surface: Athlete Seb Coe's grandfather runs in a country fair race.
explanation.walkthrough: Seb Coe is a British Olympic middle-distance champion; 'round' rearranges COE'S GRANDPA GONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's race at a country fair in which runners balance an egg on a spoon.
